drafts.gist: The claim that the Indus signs are not writing at all - contradicted by the recorded checks.
drafts.claim_plain: In a widely cited 2004 paper, Farmer, Sproat and Witzel argued that the Indus signs are not a writing system. On their view the signs do not encode spoken language at all. They are a set of non-linguistic symbols, more like emblems or traffic signs than letters or syllables.

explanation_record.ai_assistance_disclosure: This draft was written in full by an AI agent (Muse Spark, via Muse) on 2026-10-13, at the direction of Tristen Pierson. It is unauthored: no named human has adopted it, and it has no effect on the claim's stage (OD-2).
explanation_record.explanation_text: The program checked this claim against three pieces of evidence, and all three point the other way. First, published work by other researchers (Rao and colleagues, 2009) measured how predictable each sign is from the signs before it - a measure called conditional entropy. The Indus values fell inside the range seen for real language writing, and outside the range seen for non-linguistic symbol sets. Second, the program's own positional battery (Phase-43) found 20 signs that behave like word endings - they sit at the end of texts the way suffixes do. Third, the same battery found a fixed two-sign formula that opens inscriptions, the way a title or heading does. Non-linguistic emblem sets are not expected to show grammar-like habits of either kind. The claim also carries its own test on the record - it would be in trouble if the entropy data fell in the linguistic range and positional patterns rose above a random baseline - and that is the result the checks returned. On the strength of this, the program records the claim as contradicted. One caution belongs in the open: two of the three contradicting items come from the program's own test battery, run on corpora from one lineage (the Mahadevan/ICIT line). The published entropy result is the only one of the three that was produced entirely outside this program.

drafts.not_understood: Being contradicted here is narrower than it sounds. The checks argue against the strong claim that the signs encode no language at all. They do not show what language the signs encode, or what any sign says. Entropy in the linguistic range is the kind of evidence a writing system should produce, but some non-linguistic systems can produce it too, and specialists still debate the entropy result itself. The program does not know which parts of the sign system, if any, are phonetic (sound-based), and it has no check of this claim on a corpus independent of the Mahadevan/ICIT lineage. What would change the picture: a positional and entropy check on a genuinely independent corpus, and a named specialist's account that engages the suffix and title-formula findings directly.

drafts.gist: The fish sign as a badge for coastal traders - its own stated test came back against it.
drafts.claim_plain: Avishai Roif's reading says the fish sign marked a coastal guild controller or maritime trader - in plain terms, that the fish sign was a badge for people who ran sea trade, tied to the port of Lothal.

explanation_record.ai_assistance_disclosure: This draft was written in full by an AI agent (Muse Spark, via Muse) on 2026-10-13, at the direction of Tristen Pierson. It is unauthored: no named human has adopted it, and it has no effect on the claim's stage (OD-2).
explanation_record.explanation_text: This claim is one of the few in the set that carries a test sharp enough to hurt it, and the program ran that test. If the fish sign marked coastal traders, fish signs should turn up more often at coastal and maritime sites (Lothal, Dholavira) than elsewhere. The program counted fish signs across sites in its CISI-based data (the Phase-4x analysis recorded on the claim). Fish signs were not statistically enriched at coastal sites. On that result the program records the claim as partially falsified: the specific coastal prediction failed, while the wider claim about what the fish sign meant was not directly tested. One defect in the record should be stated plainly: the claim's automatic score band reads high, which points the opposite way from its falsified-leaning status. The status rests on the actual site test; the band is a consistency score computed from the record's text, and the audit flagged the conflict rather than resolving it.

drafts.not_understood: What the fish signs actually marked remains unknown - this test rules out one story about them, it does not supply another. The fish family covers several distinct signs, and the test treated them together and used the site types as published in the CISI data; a finer test, sign by sign and with better site classifications, has not been run. The claim also does not stand or fall with the fish sign's other proposed readings, which are separate claims with their own records.

drafts.gist: Parpola's claim that the script writes Proto-Dravidian by the rebus method - partly supported, on a method the program later falsified.
drafts.claim_plain: Asko Parpola's long-standing proposal says the Indus script writes an early form of the Dravidian language family (the family that today includes Tamil and Telugu). The writing is said to work by the rebus method: a picture of a thing stands for a word that sounds like the thing's name, the way a drawing of a bee could stand for the sound 'be' in English.

explanation_record.ai_assistance_disclosure: This draft was written in full by an AI agent (Muse Spark, via Muse) on 2026-10-13, at the direction of Tristen Pierson. It is unauthored: no named human has adopted it, and it has no effect on the claim's stage (OD-2).
explanation_record.explanation_text: The support on the record comes from two comparisons the program ran in its Phase-41 and Phase-43 work. Both asked the same question: if you anchor a small set of signs to Dravidian word values, do the resulting sign sequences look more probable than the same exercise done with Sanskrit values? In the first run (Phase-41, on the Mahadevan corpus of 1,669 inscriptions, five anchor signs per language), the Dravidian anchors won by a ratio of 1.0566 to 1 - a real but small margin. In the second (Phase-43, on a 1,500-sequence sample of the V3 corpus), Dravidian won by 0.484 log units per sign - again a win, again modest. That is why the status is partially supported rather than supported: the comparisons favour Dravidian over Sanskrit, but only two candidate families were compared, and the margins are small. The weakness that matters most must be stated in the open: both comparisons were computed with the program's semantic-anchoring machinery, and the program later falsified that method on held-out data (Phase-107: its predictions scored 0.000, 0 of 115). No rerun of this specific Dravidian-versus-Sanskrit comparison with a method that survived testing exists in the record. The partial support on this claim is therefore inherited from a method the program no longer trusts, and the claim's checked status has never been re-earned without it.

drafts.not_understood: Almost everything that would settle this claim is missing. There is no SA-free rerun of the language comparison. There is no test against other candidate language families or against a no-language baseline tuned the same way. The corpora used are all from the Mahadevan lineage, so there is no independent-corpus replication. And even a clean win for Dravidian over Sanskrit would not by itself establish the rebus method or any single sign reading: it would show a statistical fit, not a decipherment. What would change the picture: the same comparison rerun under a registered, SA-free method, on the strict sign set, with the rival families and margins fixed in advance.

drafts.gist: The fish sign read as 'meen' (fish/star) - one sign of the family passed its positional test; the family's commonest sign failed it.
drafts.claim_plain: Parpola's best-known single reading: the fish sign stands for the Dravidian word 'meen' - a word that means both 'fish' and 'star' - and works as the script's primary rebus sign (a picture used for its sound). The record names the Mahadevan sign numbers 72, 64 and 70 as the fish signs in question.

explanation_record.ai_assistance_disclosure: This draft was written in full by an AI agent (Muse Spark, via Muse) on 2026-10-13, at the direction of Tristen Pierson. It is unauthored: no named human has adopted it, and it has no effect on the claim's stage (OD-2).
explanation_record.explanation_text: The program's check (Phase-43, test T2.4) asked whether the signs that follow the fish sign behave the way case endings (suffixes) should if the fish sign were a word being read aloud. For Mahadevan sign 72, the answer was yes: in 181 occurrences, the sign that follows it is a text-ending sign 25.9 percent of the time, matching the pattern the test required, and the test marked it supported. But the same test tried six fish candidates, and the family's most frequent member, sign 267 (356 occurrences), failed clearly: its followers end the text only 3.8 percent of the time. The claim as written - the fish sign, as a family, is the primary rebus sign - is therefore only partly supported: one member behaves as the reading predicts, the commonest member does not. A further caution: which drawn sign counts as 'the fish sign' is itself not fully settled across the field's compilations - the program's own cross-compilation study (Phase-125) found the two great sign lists disagree far more than they agree, so a reading tied to one list's numbering carries that uncertainty with it.

drafts.not_understood: The positional test cannot show that sign 72 was pronounced 'meen' - it shows only that what follows it looks like endings. Many signs could pass such a test for unrelated reasons. The claim does not establish the star/fish wordplay, the reading of any inscription, or what the fish signs meant in the signs the test failed. What would change the picture: the same test run sign by sign across the whole fish family on the strict corpus, with the family's membership fixed in advance, and an account of why sign 267 behaves differently if the family's reading is uniform.

drafts.gist: Inscriptions follow a three-part pattern (opening, middle, ending) - the pattern is real; what the parts mean is untested.
drafts.claim_plain: Treasure A. Hunt's proposal says Indus inscriptions are built in three parts, like a form with three fields: an opening part that names identity, office or goods; a middle part about an action or transaction; and a closing part about cycles, jurisdiction or logistics.

explanation_record.ai_assistance_disclosure: This draft was written in full by an AI agent (Muse Spark, via Muse) on 2026-10-13, at the direction of Tristen Pierson. It is unauthored: no named human has adopted it, and it has no effect on the claim's stage (OD-2).
explanation_record.explanation_text: The program tested the shape of this claim, and the shape held up. In the test recorded on the claim (the positional test in the program's analysis files), 805 of 2,267 inscriptions of three or more signs followed the opening-middle-ending structure - 35.5 percent, against 0.6 percent expected by chance, a lift of about 59 times. The test also found the position-strong signs the pattern needs: 40 signs that strongly prefer the opening, 20 that strongly prefer the ending, and 61 for the middle. That is why the status is partially supported. The limit of the support is written in the test's own verdict, and it should be quoted rather than softened: the pattern is 'consistent with both Hunt model and Dravidian suffix model. Cannot distinguish between them without visual sign classification.' In other words, the check shows a three-part positional pattern exists. It does not show that the parts carry the meanings Hunt assigns them, and the same pattern is equally consistent with a rival account in which the closing signs are simply word endings in a language.

drafts.not_understood: The meanings of the three parts - identity, action, cycle - have never been tested; only their positions have. The program cannot yet say which signs are animal signs or sky signs from its own data (that needs a visual classification crosswalk it does not have), so the companion claims about animal openings and sky-sign endings are untested or only structurally supported. A three-part pattern is also weaker evidence than it may look: many record-keeping systems, linguistic or not, develop fixed field orders. What would change the picture: a visual classification of the sign classes, so the semantic version of the claim can be tested instead of the positional shadow of it.

drafts.claim_plain: A component of Hunt's three-part proposal: the animal signs - fish, unicorn, buffalo, rhinoceros, tiger, elephant - work as opening markers, standing at the start of inscriptions the way a name or title stands at the head of a form.

explanation_record.explanation_text: The record's own evidence sentence gives the honest position, and the draft keeps it intact: '40 INITIAL_STRONG signs identified; faunal-initial enrichment not yet sign-classified [STRUCTURAL SUPPORT ONLY]'. The claim's own test - animal signs enriched in opening position above a random baseline - cannot be run until the program has a visual classification of which signs are animals. drafts.gist: Sign frequencies follow the Zipf-Mandelbrot curve - the curve fits; the fit says little about what the signs mean.
drafts.claim_plain: Nisha Yadav and colleagues reported that the frequencies of Indus signs follow the Zipf-Mandelbrot pattern: a few signs are used very often, most are used rarely, and the counts between fall along one specific curve. It is the frequency pattern best known from words in real languages.

explanation_record.ai_assistance_disclosure: This draft was written in full by an AI agent (Muse Spark, via Muse) on 2026-10-13, at the direction of Tristen Pierson. It is unauthored: no named human has adopted it, and it has no effect on the claim's stage (OD-2).
explanation_record.explanation_text: The program reran this check on its V3 corpus in Phase-43 and the fit held: the recorded exponent is about 1.35, in the range the original work reported. The claim carries a proper falsifier - it fails if the frequency distribution departs from the Zipf-Mandelbrot law - and the distribution did not depart. That is the whole of the support, and it is genuine as far as it goes. Two record-keeping cautions belong with it. First, the same claim was extracted twice (from Yadav's 2009 paper and the 2010 follow-up), and for a time the program's claim set counted this one test result twice, on two records; the Phase I dedupe of 2026-10-12 merged them into this single claim, keeping the 2010 record as an evidence instance rather than a second claim. Second, the check was run by the program itself, on a corpus from the same Mahadevan lineage the original study used.

drafts.not_understood: A Zipf-style curve is weak evidence about meaning. Many systems that are not language at all - and some random processes - produce similar curves, so the fit cannot distinguish writing from non-writing, let alone identify a language. The exponent's exact value also moves with corpus size and with how signs are split or merged, and the field's compilations disagree on the sign inventory itself. What this claim does not establish: that the script encodes language, that any sign has any value, or that the corpus the curve was fitted on is complete. What would strengthen it: the same fit on an independent corpus with a sign inventory fixed in advance, reported alongside the fits for known non-linguistic symbol systems.

drafts.gist: Some signs prefer the start of texts and others the end - supported by the counts, but the claim carries no falsifier.
drafts.claim_plain: Yadav and colleagues reported that the Indus corpus has dedicated text-beginning and text-ending signs: some signs show up mostly at the start of inscriptions, others mostly at the end.

explanation_record.ai_assistance_disclosure: This draft was written in full by an AI agent (Muse Spark, via Muse) on 2026-10-13, at the direction of Tristen Pierson. It is unauthored: no named human has adopted it, and it has no effect on the claim's stage (OD-2).
explanation_record.explanation_text: The program's positional battery (Phase-43) found the pattern clearly on the V3 corpus: 40 signs that strongly prefer the opening position and 20 that strongly prefer the closing position. That is a real, reproducible feature of this corpus, and it is why the claim is recorded as strongly supported. The defect sits in the claim's own paperwork, and the audit flagged it: this record carries no falsification condition - nothing on the record states what result would have counted against the claim. A strong verdict without a stated way to be wrong is exactly the verified-but-unexplained risk this program now tracks: the counts are checked, but the claim as recorded could not have failed. Like its companion Zipf claim, this one was also double-recorded (2009 and 2010 extractions) until the Phase I dedupe merged the pair into this single claim.

drafts.not_understood: Positional preference is not meaning. Opening and closing markers appear in many symbol systems, linguistic and not, so this pattern cannot show the script encodes language. The counts also depend on where inscriptions are segmented - where one text ends and another begins - and on the sign inventory of one corpus lineage; the cross-compilation disagreement (Phase-125) means the same exercise on the other great compilation might not return the same sign sets. What would change the picture: a falsifier written onto the record, and the test rerun on the strict core and on an independent corpus with the position rules fixed in advance.

drafts.claim_plain: Avishai Roif's central thesis: the Indus script is not general writing but an economic ledger - a notation for trade guilds, tribute and guild authority - built with mnemonic shortcuts influenced by Akkadian practice.

explanation_record.explanation_text: No check has ever run on this claim. What exists on the record is the source document's own assertion, plus an automatic score computed over the record's text. The program's own evaluation note is explicit that such scores are consistency signals only and no verdict rests on them. The claim therefore stands at the first stage, created: it has been written down, and nothing more has happened to it. This claim does carry a well-formed test: it predicts the signs should cluster at sites tied to administration, trade and guild authority, and it fails if they cluster mostly at domestic or purely ritual sites instead. The program's Phase-104 evaluation found the test cannot be run with the data in the repository: the corpus carries site names but no classification of sites by type (gateway, border, administrative, domestic), and no such dataset exists in the repo. The thesis is also a bundle of several claims at once - ledger function, guild authority, Akkadian influence - and no one part of it has been separated out and tested on its own.

drafts.not_understood: Everything about this claim is not understood, in the plain sense that nothing about it has been tested. The specific missing piece is named data: a classification of excavation sites by function that scholars would accept. Without it, the distribution test the claim itself proposes cannot run. The Akkadian-influence part additionally needs contact evidence this program does not hold. A favourable distribution, if it were ever shown, would still not establish the ledger reading of any single inscription.

drafts.gist: The site association survives controlling for preservation and text composition - but not for time. That rider is part of the result.
drafts.claim_plain: G1 is the controlled version of the F3 claim. F3 found that in the ICIT-lineage corpus, sites use different sign repertoires - but sites also differ in preservation and in what kinds of texts survive. G1 asks: does the site association survive once preservation and text composition are held fixed?

explanation_record.explanation_text: The check (Phase-140) re-ran the F3 test with the shuffling done inside groups matched for composition and preservation (preservation was recorded for 99.9 percent of the rows, which is what made the control possible). The observed statistic, 4966.36, stood far above the shuffled values (typical value 2684.74); not one of 9,999 shuffles reached it (p = 0.0001). The Spec 026 rerun (Phase-385) confirmed the effect size: the interval [0.184, 0.210] lies entirely above the declared margin, so SUPPORTED under control stands. The rider, which the program requires wherever this result is stated and which this draft states in the body, not a footnote: chronology is not controlled in the primary test. Sites' period mixes differ, and until period is held fixed the same way, part of what is called a site effect may be a time effect - later and earlier cities are not the same cities. A chronology sensitivity bound is reported alongside the result, but it is not the controlled verdict.

drafts.not_understood: The uncontrolled-chronology rider is the not-understood core of this claim: the program cannot yet say how much of the surviving association is place and how much is period. Also open: the mechanism (genuinely different local repertoires versus different mixes of text genres that composition control only partly captures), and the standing disagreement with the Holdat layer, where no effect of the required size was found. The claim does not establish population movement; the movement question was asked separately (Spec 027 Stage 1) and came back inconclusive. What would change the picture: the primary test re-run with period strata from a chronology spine strong enough to support it - the Spec 030 extension tried to build exactly that spine and closed negative, so the limiting factor is dated material, not method.

drafts.gist: Do cities with similar sign repertoires sit closer together? A real but tiny signal that collapses without Harappa - inconclusive.
drafts.claim_plain: Stage 1 of the movement study asked whether a site's sign repertoire resembles the repertoires of nearby sites more than distant ones - the pattern you would expect if people, goods and habits moved between neighbouring places. The contract was frozen and registered publicly (OSF, osf.io/pnqrx) before the test ran.

explanation_record.explanation_text: The primary result: site similarity accounts for a small share of the differences between repertoires - median adjusted R-squared 0.01677, that is about 1.7 percent of the variation, with interval [0.01032, 0.02397]. The signal is consistent (the rejection share was 1.000, and both controls passed: the negative control sat near zero, the positive control behaved as designed). But the frozen SUPPORTED rule also required the result to survive leaving any one site out, and removing Harappa dropped the median to 0.00928 - below the 0.01 margin fixed in advance. The CONTRADICTED rule did not fire either. The verdict is therefore INCONCLUSIVE, exactly as the frozen rules produce it. A sensitivity version restricted to complete cases read slightly higher (0.01793) and carried no verdict. The study's own record also notes what could not be run at all: the planned Parpola-numbering sensitivity was not estimable, because the crosswalk covers only 17.57 percent of the relevant signs.

drafts.not_understood: The jackknife failure is the not-understood core: the program cannot tell whether Harappa carries the signal because Harappa is genuinely central, or because its corpus is so much larger than the others that it dominates any pooled measure. A 1.7-percent association also cannot carry a movement story by itself - shared period, shared trade goods and shared excavation practices all predict the same small resemblance. Stage 2 of the movement study was not executed as a stage, and the timing question behind it (Q6) remains not-yet-testable even after the chronology-spine extension (Spec 030, Phase-394) closed negative. What would change the picture: the Harappa-specific follow-up arms (Spec 028, drafted alongside this one) are the program's own answer to the jackknife problem - and both came back inconclusive as well, which is itself the current state of knowledge.

explanation_record.explanation_text: The headline number is the strongest in the movement line: median adjusted R-squared 0.02237, interval [0.01222, 0.03333] - entirely above the 0.01 margin - with a rejection share of 0.955.
